description: Audited communication-round counts for universal constant-round algorithms. A number is a source-stated schedule or the unchanged schedule of a reanalyzed algorithm. The ≤ sign marks a conservative implementation bound reconstructed from the source. Unspecified totals and inaccessible full algorithms retain Constant. Counts do not assert minimum possible round complexity; initial-information conventions are recorded in the evidence.

entries.explanation: Lemma 6.1 explicitly states six rounds and gives the schedule: rounds 1–2 learn identifiers within distance two; round 3 announces membership in D; rounds 4–5 compute and exchange residual degrees; round 6 notifies chosen dominators. The algorithm uses unique identifiers and unrestricted LOCAL messages, without a supplied embedding or degree bound.

With r = 1, this adds four rounds to the six-round planar dominating-set algorithm explicitly used in the paper, giving at most ten rounds in total. This is an upper bound for that composition, not a minimum-round claim. Inputs are connected, unweighted planar graphs with distinct identifiers.

entries.explanation: Algorithm 1 explicitly uses the first round to exchange local degrees. Each vertex then selects itself if its degree is at least four or if it has no neighbor of degree at least four. The source assumes incident ports and local degree are initially available. Neither identifiers nor an embedding are needed.

entries.explanation: In round 1, vertices broadcast their degree and random tie-breaking value. In round 2, each vertex marks a neighbor of maximum weight. The repeat loop is absent when m = 0. The selected vertices give total domination and hence ordinary domination. Vertices initially know their neighbors; the source excludes isolated vertices.

entries.explanation: The same m = 0 algorithm uses two rounds: broadcast weights, then mark a maximum-weight neighbor. Theorem 2.1 gives factor 16 against the total-domination optimum. Vertices initially know their neighbors, and isolated vertices are excluded.

evidence.title: Primary source communication schedule
evidence.location: Algorithm 1 lines 1–2 and Theorem 2.1; arXiv v2 PDF p. 3

entries.explanation: A conservative sequential count is 3 + 7 + 1 = 11: two rounds to inspect radius-two neighborhoods and one to mark neighbors of D1; then two neighborhood exchanges, two rounds to compute sequences, two to report their endpoints, and one to mark neighbors of D2; finally, the source includes a last selection step. This includes that final step conservatively and does not claim an optimized schedule. The algorithm uses distinct identifiers and a supplied upper bound on depth-one density.

evidence.title: Primary source communication schedule
evidence.location: Section 2, PDF pp. 6–7; Section 6, PDF p. 15; corrected arXiv v3

entries.explanation: Rounds 1–2: exchange identifiers then neighbor lists; decide phase-one set D using adjacencies from N(v) to candidate vertices in N²(v). Round 3: broadcast D membership; each vertex knows whether it lies in N[D]. Round 4: broadcast uncovered flags; each vertex computes residual closed-neighborhood degree. Round 5: broadcast residual degrees; each uncovered vertex chooses its dominator. Round 6: notify selected neighbors; all vertices know final membership. The source initially gives only each vertex its own ID. Unbounded LOCAL messages permit the lists. Auxiliary density c and excluded-depth-one-minor t affect local computation/analysis, not communication phases.

entries.explanation: First round selects vertices of degree at least six. Second round adds vertices outside the first set that are not yet 2-dominated. Source also allows one round to obtain own degree. A conservative two-round implementation obtains degree by dummy messages in round 1, then exchanges high-degree flags in round 2 and decides output. Messages are one bit.

evidence.title: Primary source algorithm
evidence.location: Section 2, Algorithm 1, first explanatory paragraph

entries.explanation: Rounds 1–2 obtain neighbor lists and decide D1 by radius-two information. Round 3 broadcasts D1; compute two-domination flags Z. Round 4 broadcasts Z; compute residual open-neighborhood degrees. Round 5 broadcasts these degrees; vertices outside Z choose one or two neighbors as prescribed. Round 6 notifies the chosen neighbors. Distinct IDs in the source LOCAL model; unbounded messages. All thresholds are fixed numerical constants for excluded TK4,4.

evidence.title: Primary source algorithm
evidence.location: Procedure 2 PDF p. 6; radius-two remark p. 7; Theorem 7 p. 8

entries.explanation: Round 1 obtains the local degree if necessary and tests the threshold L. Round 2 exchanges threshold-membership flags; every unselected vertex with fewer than k selected neighbors then selects itself. The fixed parameters g and k determine L through local computation. The approximation factor depends on them, while this communication bound does not.

evidence.location: Procedure 1 PDF p. 5; Corollary 3 p. 6

entries.explanation: The same threshold procedure uses at most two rounds: obtain the local degree if necessary, then exchange selection flags and add vertices with fewer than k selected neighbors. The source uses fixed k ≥ 3 and h = 4. These parameters affect the local threshold and approximation factor, not the number of rounds.

evidence.title: Primary source algorithm
evidence.location: Procedure 1 PDF p. 5; Corollary 2 p. 6

entries.explanation: The paper gives two phases without a total round count. A conservative implementation floods identifiers and neighbor lists for six rounds, then uses one round to notify selected neighbors. The first six rounds reveal degrees through distance five, sufficient to reconstruct the first selection and uncovered vertices within distance two. Every replacement candidate covers the selecting vertex, so it lies in its closed neighborhood. This is an implementation upper bound, not a source-stated or optimal count.

entries.explanation: Theorem C and Corollary 1.1 give universal constant-round algorithms for these fixed graph classes. Section 6.5, Theorem 6.13, bounds the fractional algorithm by fixed parameters, but gives no end-to-end numerical total. The partition in Lemma 6.9 also uses parameter-dependent constants without numerical instantiation. The three broadcasts after the fractional stage in Section 5.4 are only the final stage, not the total round count.

entries.explanation: The supplied weak two-colouring permits the Section 4 star-forest construction in an absolute constant number of rounds. The four-round schedule below computes exactly its final star centres without communicating the final edge orientations. Every black vertex with white children becomes a centre. An original white root remains a centre exactly when at least one of its black children has no white children. A white vertex that proposed to a black vertex is a leaf. In the all-depth-two case a root chooses one child for edge reversal, but the choice does not affect the set of centres, so the dominating-set output needs no extra round. This is an implementation upper bound derived from the paper, not a printed exact runtime or a claim of round optimality. Δ occurs in the approximation guarantee, not in the communication radius. The catalogue’s f(Δ) classification can be strengthened to constant. Schedule: (1) exchange weak-colouring bits; (2) black vertices propose to white parents; (3) white vertices without black children propose to black parents; (4) black vertices report whether they acquired white children. The selected set is the final star centres.
